claims.text: Anodic potential cycling between approximately 0.6 and 1.0 V vs. RHE forms a sub-monolayer or thin Pt-oxide layer on the catalyst surface.
The anodically induced Pt-oxide layer is stabilized under the subsequent ethanol-oxidation conditions.
The Pt-oxide layer alters the adsorption energies of ethanol and its partial-oxidation intermediates.
The altered surface facilitates removal of poisoning intermediates.
The Pt-oxide layer favors complete 12-electron oxidation of ethanol to CO2 over incomplete oxidation pathways.
Surface oxidation suppresses accumulation of adsorbed carbon monoxide or other deactivating species.
Suppressing poisoning intermediates increases ethanol-oxidation current density.
Suppressing poisoning intermediates slows catalyst degradation during operation.
The pre-treated catalyst will exhibit higher ethanol-oxidation current density than the untreated catalyst.
The pre-treated catalyst will exhibit a greater CO2-to-acetaldehyde product ratio than the untreated catalyst.
The pre-treated catalyst will show less current decay over time than the untreated catalyst.
The hypothesized benefit applies in acidic aqueous media at moderate potentials of approximately 0.7–0.9 V vs. RHE where the thin oxide is maintained.
The hypothesized benefit may fail at lower overpotentials because oxide formation is minimal.
The hypothesized benefit may fail at excessively high potentials because thicker oxides or catalyst dissolution can occur.
The appropriate control is the same catalyst without anodic cycling, tested under otherwise identical ethanol-oxidation conditions.
Observation of a Pt-oxide layer without a corresponding performance enhancement would falsify the proposed oxide-mediated explanation.
